title: APAC Gold Market Insights: Gold allocation in different Chinese economic cycles
author: @goldcouncil
text:
Ray Jia

Hanyang Ye

26 November, 2026

SummaryChina’s economy remains in a structural transition, as weakness in traditional growth engines, such as real estate, weighs on momentum while fast-growing new sectors including high-tech sectors are not yet large enough to fully offset the slowdownIn different economic cycles, local assets exhibit different characteristics; thus, while a strategic allocation to Chinese portfolios can be useful over the long-term, local investors could benefit from adjusting allocations across cycles, with weights ranging from 5% to 28%Amidst the ongoing economic transition, we may stay in the current cycle for a while, which requires a higher gold allocation to help maximum Sharpe improvement of a hypothetical Chinese portfolioIn the past quarter, China’s investment demand remained strong; jewellery consumption picked up seasonally though remained below the long-term average; and the local central bank ramped up its gold addition

China’s ongoing economic transitionChina’s economy is passing through an extended period of structural adjustment (Chart 1). A main driver of the slowing trend in China’s growth in recent years is China’s transitioning from traditional sectors-led growth to a high-quality and new-tech led one.1 And the contribution from traditional growth engines has been diminishing while new quality productive forces, while rising rapidly, are yet to become large enough to provide broad-based momentum.For instance, the real estate sector has experienced sustained weakness: both residential home starts and home sales continued to tumble during the first three quarters.2 In contrast, high-tech sectors have grown rapidly, with their value-add rising 14% y/y between January and September, compared to 5% across all industries (Chart 2). And in-between the transitioning phases of growth models, China’s economy is exhibiting signs of a slowdown.

Asset allocation implicationsChinese assets tend to perform differently across cycles. In the slowdown phase, also characterised by lowering interest rates and yet tepid borrowing, investors’ risk appetite tends to be subdued. Local equities typically weaken amid soft growth and constrained corporate earnings, while defensive assets such as government bonds and gold outperform as yields usually fall and safe-haven demand rises.Gold, in RMB, however delivers strong returns in all four cycles (Chart 3). It is mainly driven by two of gold’s distinctive aspects. First, its dual nature as both a consumer good and an investment asset: economic expansion can support jewellery and technology fabrication – cyclical component – while periods of uncertainty strengthen investor interest – counter-cyclical factors, resulting in demand stability over time. Second, gold is a global asset with diverse demand spreading across the globe, suggesting its performance not solely driven by economic conditions in any single country. These characteristics have led to gold’s robust performances in different economic cycles and averaged a compound annual growth return of 9% over the past 20 years, outpacing other assets.RMB gold’s correlation with equities is similarly useful for investors (Chart 4). Amidst gold and local equities’ different return profiles across different cycles, their correlation turns negative during periods of economic stress, helping investors diversify risks; and it flips positive in a prosperity environment, preserving local portfolios’ upside potential.

What’s the proper ratio of gold allocation for Chinese investors?This dynamic relationship suggests a two-layer allocation approach: a strategic allocation that captures gold’s ability to generate returns and diversify risks across economic cycles; and a layer of allocation adjustment in different cycles. In this way, gold can contribute to portfolio returns in favourable conditions while providing greater diversification and downside protection when it is needed most.Back-testing historical data of a hypothetical Chinese basic pension portfolio with 35% equities, 55% bonds and 10% cash suggests that a 16% allocation to gold – while proportionally reducing other assets’ weights – can maximise the marginal improvement in the portfolio’s Sharpe ratio in all economic cycles (Chart 6).We focus on marginal improvement rather than the absolute Sharpe ratio because gold has delivered exceptionally strong returns in China since 2004, when data of local stocks and bonds become available. And a purely Sharpe-maximising portfolio would require a gold allocation of more than 50% (Chart 5), which is unrealistic for most investors. Assessing the marginal improvement therefore provides a more practical indication of where gold’s additional risk-adjusted return benefits begin to diminish.

Perhaps a more relevant question is: what is the proper allocation to gold in the current economic cycle? To answer this, we first take a step back and consider what a portfolio should aim to achieve across different cycles. We believe an appropriate framework is to prioritise risk reduction during bad times – i.e. to maximise the marginal improvement in Sharpe ratio, while maintaining upside potential in expansionary periods, when equities tend to perform best – we select an upside return capture ratio of 98% (see notes under Chart 8).The results are intuitive (Chart 7). During periods of slowdown, investors would need to raise their gold allocation to around 21% to maximise the marginal improvement in the portfolio’s Sharpe, rising further to 28% in stagnant. These findings are consistent with the asset performance and gold correlation dynamics discussed above.During economic recoveries and expansion, adding gold still reduces overall portfolio volatility and improves its Sharpe ratio, but at the cost of some return. To maintain at least 98% return participation, our analysis suggests gold allocations of around 11% during recoveries and 5% during expansion (Chart 8). At these levels, investors could preserve most of the portfolio’s upside participation while still improving their Sharpe ratio.

In addition to economic cycles, we also back tested the allocation of gold maximising marginal Sharpe ratio improvement (Chart 9) – in the same hypothetical portfolio. This is mainly to avoid potential bias of selection in economic cycles. Results show that this hypothetical Chinese portfolio needs between 9% and 16% gold to realize peak Sharpe ratio improvement in the past 5, 10, 15,20 and 22 – the full sample – years (Chart 10).

The gold demand picture in China during Q3In Q3, retail gold demand in China totalled 192t (Chart 11), 24% higher q/q and a 12% y/y rise. Bar and coin investment stayed robust at 79t (+7% y/y, -26% q/q), well above the 10-year Q3 average of 65t; jewellery consumption improved seasonally, rising 30% q/q to 66t (-22% y/y); local gold ETFs saw inflows of 27t, reversing the Q2 loss of 22t; industrial demand stayed stable at 20t.The PBoC reported an addition of 63t of gold in Q3, its strongest quarter since Q3 2022 (Chart 12), and remained among the most active official gold buyers globally so far this year. This lifted Chinese central bank’s y-t-d purchases to 103t and official gold holdings to 2,410t, or 8.5% of total reserves.
